lesson_title: The Ramp, the Fire and the Wedge: Where Rain Comes From
hook_text: Every raindrop in history was made by one of three machines.
clip_script: Every raindrop in history was made the same way: air went up, cooled, filled to the brim, and let go. The only question is — what sent the air up? Three lifting machines. The ramp is a mountain range: wet sea air hits the rock wall and has exactly one exit, upward. It cools on the climb, tips its water down the side facing the wind, and rolls down the far slope warm and dry — one side drips while the other side rations water. The fire is the summer ground itself: on a January afternoon the earth bakes until the air lifts off like heat over a braai, cloud stacks into a dark tower, and around four o'clock the tower breaks — twenty minutes of furious rain, sometimes drowning one farm while the neighbouring one stays bone dry. The wedge is cold air on the move: heavier cold air slides underneath the warm moist air like a splitting wedge under a log, heaving it off the ground, and rain falls along the whole moving boundary — the Cape's entire winter, wedge after wedge off the Atlantic. Ramp, fire, wedge. Three machines, one recipe.
visual_style: Three quick animated dioramas: a cross-section mountain with rain streaking one flank, shimmering thermals stacking a dark tower over farmland, and a blue wedge of cold air prising a warm layer off the ground.
mood: Mechanical and satisfying — rain revealed as engineering.
pacing: One brisk chapter per machine, each ending on its name, closing with the three names drummed in sequence.
call_to_action: Take the full lesson and match every rainy day to the machine that built it.
